chunks: More than one (narrator) narrated to us from one of the two of them (peace be upon them both) that he said:
The servant cannot be a believer until he recognizes God, His Messenger, and all the Imams, and the Imam of his time, and refers (all matters) to him and submits to him.
Then he said: How can he recognize the last one while he is ignorant of the first?

key_terms.إِمَامَ زَمَانِهِ: Imam of his time — the living, currently authoritative Imam, not a past one
key_terms.مُؤْمِن: Believer (Momin) — one whose faith is complete and operative
key_terms.يَرُدَّ إِلَيْهِ: Refers matters to him — practical submission, bringing decisions and questions to the Imam
key_terms.يَعْرِفَ: To recognize/know (ma'rifa) — deeper than mere information, implies personal acknowledgment and acceptance
key_terms.يُسَلِّمَ لَهُ: Submits to him — full acquiescence to the Imam's authority

ai.seo_question: What does it mean to recognize the Imam of one's time in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith from either Imam al-Baqir or Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon them) establishes that true faith requires recognition (ma'rifa) of God, the Prophet, all the Imams, and specifically the living Imam of one's own time, with active submission and referral of matters to him. The final rhetorical question — how can one recognize the last Imam while ignorant of the first? — underscores the sequential necessity of acknowledging the entire chain of Imamate, as each Imam's authority derives from and continues the one before. This teaching was directed at Shia Muslims in the formative period of the Imamate doctrine, clarifying that faith is not merely abstract belief but involves a living, practical relationship with the current Imam.
word_analysis: one of the two of them
